blocks.text: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterised by destruction of pancreatic beta cells, resulting in absolute or near-absolute insulin deficiency. Patients require lifelong insulin replacement to prevent hyperglycaemia, diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and death.
Unlike type 2 diabetes, T1DM is not primarily caused by insulin resistance. It can occur at any age, although it commonly presents during childhood and adolescence.

blocks.text: Some patients experience a temporary partial remission called the honeymoon phase, during which insulin requirements decrease because residual beta-cell function temporarily improves. Insulin must not be discontinued.

blocks.text: Important: Insulin is essential even when the patient is fasting or unwell. Basal insulin must not be omitted in established T1DM. Prandial insulin is adjusted according to food intake and the applicable sick-day plan.

blocks.title: The preferred conventional treatment is a combination of:

items.text: Basal insulin: provides background insulin throughout the day and night.
Prandial insulin: controls the rise in glucose following meals.
Correction insulin: additional rapid-acting insulin to correct hyperglycaemia when indicated.

blocks.caption: This is also called multiple daily injection (MDI) therapy.

blocks.text: Duration varies with dose, preparation and individual response.
Preferred options: Glargine or degludec are commonly used for once-daily basal coverage. NPH is an alternative where cost or availability limits access to insulin analogues.

Rapid-acting insulin analogues can generally be administered immediately before eating. Some products permit administration shortly after starting a meal under specific circumstances, according to their product instructions.

content_groups.group_title: 4.4 Alternative treatment: Continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion

blocks.text: Insulin pump therapy delivers rapid-acting insulin continuously through a subcutaneous infusion system.

items.text: Integration with CGM in automated insulin delivery systems.

blocks.text: Automated insulin delivery systems combine insulin pumps, CGM and algorithms to adjust insulin delivery.
These systems are particularly useful for selected patients with recurrent hypoglycaemia, variable glucose levels or difficulty achieving glycaemic targets.

Premixed insulin is generally not preferred for T1DM because it offers less flexibility in matching insulin requirements to food intake.
Guideline position: The ADA 2026 recommends MDI or insulin pump therapy for most adults with T1DM and generally favours insulin analogues over injectable human insulin to reduce hypoglycaemia risk.

Every patient with T1DM should receive structured diabetes education.
A. Insulin adherence

items.text: Never discontinue basal insulin, even during fasting or illness.
Do not independently make major changes to insulin doses.
Understand the difference between basal, prandial and correction insulin.

blocks.text: B. Dietary advice

items.text: Avoid excessive consumption of sugar-sweetened drinks.
Avoid skipping meals after administering meal insulin.

blocks.text: C. Exercise
Exercise improves insulin sensitivity but can cause hypoglycaemia.

items.text: Discuss insulin adjustment for planned physical activity.
Avoid exercise when significant ketonaemia is present.

blocks.text: D. Sick-day rules
This is one of the most important aspects of T1DM education.

blocks.title: During fever, vomiting, diarrhoea or infection:

items.text: Check blood glucose frequently, commonly every 2–4 hours.
Check blood ketones when glucose is persistently elevated or whenever unwell.
Use additional correction insulin only according to the prescribed sick-day plan.
Seek urgent medical attention for persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, difficulty breathing, confusion or inability to maintain hydration.

blocks.text: Blood ketones of 1.5 mmol/L or above require urgent clinical advice and assessment; levels of 3 mmol/L or above strongly suggest significant ketosis and warrant emergency assessment.
E. Driving

items.text: Follow local driving regulations regarding diabetes.

blocks.text: F. Foot care

items.text: Seek assessment for ulcers, infection or changes in foot colour.

blocks.text: G. Medical identification
Patients should carry medical identification stating that they have type 1 diabetes and use insulin.

blocks.text: Important points to remember

items.text: T1DM is caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells.
Basal–bolus insulin is the standard conventional injection regimen.
Insulin analogues generally have a lower hypoglycaemia risk than human insulin.
The honeymoon phase does not mean diabetes has resolved.
Never stop basal insulin during an intercurrent illness.
GAD65, IA-2 and ZnT8 antibodies support autoimmune T1DM.
Renal impairment can reduce insulin requirements.
Glucagon is important in managing severe hypoglycaemia outside hospital.
Pregnancy usually increases insulin requirements as gestation progresses, followed by a marked fall after delivery.
DKA is a potentially fatal consequence of significant insulin deficiency.
